related_questions.question: How to test for poison in the body?

text_blocks.snippet: To test for the presence of poison in the body, a doctor can order a toxicology screen, which typically involves blood or urine tests. These tests analyze bodily fluids for the presence and concentration of various substances, including drugs, heavy metals, and other toxins.
snippet_highlighted_words: a doctor can order a toxicology screen, which typically involves blood or urine tests

list.snippet: The doctor will first review the patient's medical history and conduct a physical examination to assess potential exposure and symptoms.

list.title: Toxicology Screen:
list.snippet: This is a common test that screens for a wide range of substances, including common drugs, using urine or saliva samples, according to familydoctor.org.

list.title: Specific Toxin Tests:
list.snippet: Depending on the suspected poison, specific blood or urine tests may be ordered. For example, lead levels can be tested with a blood test, according to Testing.com.

list.title: Other Samples:
list.snippet: In some cases, other samples like fingernails or hair may be used to detect certain toxins, says Testing.com.

list.title: ECG:
list.snippet: An electrocardiogram (ECG or EKG) can help detect heart rhythm abnormalities that might be caused by poisoning.

list.title: X-rays:
list.snippet: X-rays can help identify ingested objects like batteries, according to NYU Langone Health.

list.title: CT/MRI Scans:
list.snippet: In rare cases, these scans may be used to assess the effects of poisoning on the brain.
The doctor will interpret the test results to determine the type and concentration of the poison, if any, and assess the impact on the patient's health.
The concentration of a substance in the blood is often used to gauge the severity of toxicity, says Britannica.
The best way to prevent poisoning is to avoid contact with harmful substances, says familydoctor.org.

related_questions.question: What to do if you think you've been poisoned?

text_blocks.snippet: If you suspect you've been poisoned, seek immediate medical help. Call emergency services or go to the nearest emergency room. Provide as much information as possible to healthcare providers, including what you think the poison is, when and how it was ingested, and any symptoms you're experiencing.

list.snippet: Call 911 or your local emergency number immediately.
Go to the nearest emergency room.
Do not wait for symptoms to worsen.
Identify the poison if possible: If you know what you ingested, try to provide details about the substance, its packaging, and any instructions on the label.
When did it happen? Inform them about the timing of the exposure.
How was it ingested? Specify whether it was swallowed, inhaled, or absorbed through the skin.
Any symptoms? Describe the symptoms you are experiencing, such as nausea, vomiting, dizziness, difficulty breathing, etc.
What first aid was given? If you or someone else tried to provide first aid, let them know.

text_blocks.snippet: 3. Specific Actions Based on Exposure Type:

list.snippet: Do not induce vomiting unless instructed by a medical professional or poison control.
If you vomit, try to save a sample of the vomit for analysis.
If the person is conscious, give them sips of water or milk to dilute the poison.
Move the person to fresh air immediately if it is safe to do so.
If the person is unconscious, call for help and wait for professional assistance.
Remove any contaminated clothing.
Rinse the affected skin with lukewarm water for at least 15 minutes.
Rinse the affected eye with lukewarm water for at least 15 to 20 minutes.
Do not try to neutralize the poison with other substances (e.g., lemon juice, vinegar) unless directed by poison control.
Do not try to induce vomiting unless instructed by medical professionals.
Do not give anything by mouth to an unconscious person.
Keep all medications and chemicals out of reach of children.
Store chemicals in their original containers with proper labels.
Be careful when handling potentially toxic substances.
Keep the Poison Help line (1-800-222-1222) handy in case of emergencies, according to HRSA Poison Help (.gov).
